Line 98: "Bad, because nesting depth and loader memory stay unbounded until Open questions this ADR requests from the Configuration model close; depth would be checked over `lexer.Tokenize` output (RZ-CFG-001)." Line 50: "Rejects non-UTF-8, byte order marks and oversize input (RZ-CFG-001; ...), duplicate keys (RZ-CFG-002), anchors, aliases, merge keys (RZ-CFG-003) and custom tags (RZ-CFG-004)". Line 30: "**Bounded input**: nothing that can exhaust memory or change unreviewed values." Configuration model, Error codes: "RZ-CFG-001 | Parse error, non-UTF-8, byte order mark, or size limit".
blocking.fix: Line 50: change "oversize input (RZ-CFG-001;" to "oversize or over-deep input, depth checked over `lexer.Tokenize` output before parsing (RZ-CFG-001;". Line 98: replace the bullet with "Bad, because the depth limit's value and peak loader memory (hypothesis) stay unset until the Configuration model adds an Open question for them." Line 92: replace "size limits, and a depth limit once decided, bound the rest" with "size and depth limits bound the rest". The net change is about -2 words. The Open question request is recorded under foundation_amendments.

Research section 6 and the Tech stack row record no go directive for goccy/go-yaml. Cite its go.mod once research adds it, or write 'S2 verified for jsonschema/v6, Pending CI for goccy/go-yaml'.
'loader memory stay unbounded' overstates the gap. The 64 MiB and 20,000-resource limits already bound memory. What is missing is a stated multiple of source size. The L1-2 rewording fixes this.

YAML 1.2 allows tabs only as separation space, never as indentation, and goccy/go-yaml's scanner has a history of rejecting tabs. Name the fallback if the tab fixture fails on day one: a JSON front end in the same loader that emits the same AST and source map.

Still open from the prior round. RFC 8785 serializes numbers as IEEE 754 doubles, so schema integers above 2^53 can collide in the digest. Ask the Configuration model, through an Open question, to cap schema integers at 2^53-1 or carry them as strings.

blocking.section: Decision outcome, Libraries row (line 53); Confirmation, Loader conformance suite (line 104)
blocking.issue: The ADR says every substituted value is typed by the YAML 1.2 core schema, whatever the target field's type. The owning document says something different. Substitution runs on parsed string scalars, and only a value that is exactly one expression is re-typed, by the rendered schema view, so the type comes from the target field. In a string field, the value stays a string. The authoring view also allows the substituted string form only for non-string fields. Under the ADR's rule, `exact: ${CANARY}` with CANARY=true becomes a boolean and fails RZ-CFG-005, a substituted `0777` in a header value or path becomes the integer 777, a substituted `null` removes the field, and a partial expression such as `v${X}` would be re-typed although the owning document never re-types it. The fixture requires a substituted `0777` to decode as decimal 777 with no condition on the field type, so the CI gate enforces the contradiction.
blocking.evidence: line 53: "Ruralz types plain scalars from token text by the YAML 1.2 core schema (null, true/false, decimal, `0o` and `0x` integers, floats, else string), also after substitution, never by library typing."; line 104: "plain scalars `yes`, `on`, `0777`, `0b1`, `1_000` and `2026-09-23`, raw and substituted: `0777` MUST decode as decimal 777, the rest as strings."; Configuration model, Environment substitution: "String values MAY contain `${VAR}` ... on parsed scalars only, so it cannot inject structure ... A value that is exactly one expression is re-typed by the rendered schema view (`port: ${HTTPS_PORT:-8443}` becomes an integer)"; Schema keywords that drive tooling: "The authoring view ... lets every non-string scalar that permits substitution also be a string matching `^\$\{...\}$`."
blocking.fix: Line 53: replace "also after substitution, never by library typing" with "never by library typing; a whole-value `${VAR}` result is typed so for non-string schema fields only". Line 104: replace "raw and substituted: `0777` MUST decode as decimal 777, the rest as strings" with "raw, or substituted into an integer field: `0777` MUST decode as 777, the rest as strings". Add one fixture that substitutes `0777` into a string field and requires the string "0777". blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling)
blocking.issue: New regression from the revision. The success cache is now flushed on every snapshot swap and every revocation advance, but the Node hashes only 10 to 20 credentials per second per slot, with max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) slots and 4 x slots waiters. (1) The revocation flush is not needed: in Figure 2 a cache hit still passes the revocation check (E to F), yet each new `jti`, cut-off or key entry anywhere in the Cluster empties every basic-auth cache on every Node. At one logout revocation per second (hypothesis), the cache never warms, and `auth.basic` throughput falls to the raw hash rate, about 20 to 40 requests per second on an 8-core Node (hypothesis). (2) The swap flush turns every Hot Reload into a burst of RZ-AUTH-007. With 1,000 active basic-auth clients on an 8-core Node (2 slots, 8 waiters), about 990 get 429 at once after the swap, and recovery takes about 25 to 50 s (hypothesis). A Zero-Downtime Upgrade does the same, and it also empties the username LRU, whose new-bucket rate is capped at 100 per second (target). (3) The steady-state capacity is not stated. Entries last 60 s and hits do not extend them, so a Node supports about 60 x hash rate active basic-auth clients: 1,200 to 2,400 on 8 cores (hypothesis), well below the 10,000-entry cache (target). Beyond that, legitimate clients get 429 with no attack at all. (4) 'hashing uses at most a quarter of the cores' is false when GOMAXPROCS is below 4: on a 2-vCPU Node, max(1, 2/4) = 1 slot is half the CPU.
blocking.evidence: Line 402: "| Success cache | HMAC-SHA-256 under a per-process key; 60 s from verification, not extended by hits; 64 shards, 10,000 entries per Node (target); flushed on each snapshot swap and revocation advance; a hit skips throttle and hash |"; line 404: "| Hash queue | max(1, `GOMAXPROCS`/4) slots, which cap the Node's hash rate; 4 × slots waiters, 1 s deadline (target); overflow gets RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed |"; line 409: "At 600,000 iterations a slot verifies 10 to 20 credentials per second (hypothesis), so hashing uses at most a quarter of the cores"; Figure 2: "E -- \"yes\" --> F{\"On the revocation list?\"}".
blocking.fix: (1) Stop flushing on revocation advance, since the revocation check already runs after a cache hit, and say so. (2) On a snapshot swap, keep each entry whose username and stored credential digest are unchanged in the new snapshot, for example by adding the Consumer credential digest to the cache key, and evict only changed or removed credentials. (3) State the steady-state capacity, active basic-auth clients per Node = 60 s x slots x 10 to 20 per second (hypothesis). Also state the post-restart ramp under the 100 per second new-bucket rate (target), and whether a new-bucket overflow returns RZ-AUTH-007 with `Retry-After`. Consider refreshing an entry on a hit up to a hard maximum age, for example 15 minutes (target). (4) Write 'at most a quarter of the cores when GOMAXPROCS is 4 or more, otherwise one core'.

blocking.section: Revocation (Expiry)
blocking.issue: New regression from the revision. `kid` entries now expire after the maximum token lifetime (24 hours (target)), which contradicts T2. An attacker who holds a leaked IdP private key can mint tokens with any `exp`. A `kid` entry evicts the key only until the next JWKS refresh returns it, and blocks tokens signed with it only while the entry exists. So if the IdP still publishes the key 24 hours after revocation, the leaked key is valid again on every Node, with no alert. The expiry therefore does not end the key's risk, and the T2 mitigation 'kid revocation' stops working after one day.
blocking.evidence: Line 426: "**Expiry.** A `jti` entry MUST carry the token's `exp`, capped at the maximum lifetime, and expires then; cut-offs and `kid` entries expire after that lifetime, and a cut-off meanwhile refuses the subject's tokens without `iat`."; line 92: "| T2 | JWT forgery, leaked IdP key | TB-1, TB-10 | [JWT and OIDC](#jwt-and-oidc); `kid` [revocation](#revocation) |"; line 173: "a `kid` [revocation](#revocation) entry evicts a leaked key."
blocking.fix: Make a `kid` entry permanent until the key leaves the issuer's JWKS. Nodes refuse to load a revoked (issuer, `kid`) from any JWKS fetch and report whether the key is still served. Ruralz Control collects the entry only after no Node has seen the key for one maximum lifetime, and it raises a degraded state and an alert while the IdP still publishes it. Give `kid` entries a small sub-cap within the 100,000 entries, for example 1,000 (target), and let operators remove them manually, with an audited `credential.revoked` collection event.

non_blocking.suggestion: Each entry still carries its own signature. A Node cold-starting or reconnecting against a list near the 100,000-entry cap (target) then verifies up to 100,000 signatures, several seconds of one core (hypothesis). Have the signed high-water mark cover a digest or Merkle root of the entry set, so that a full snapshot needs one verification.

'One shared bucket ... so timing reveals nothing' does not hold under load. An attacker who drains the shared unknown-username bucket then gets an immediate RZ-AUTH-007 for unknown names and a hashed 401 for known ones, which enumerates usernames. Either give unknown usernames per-name buckets derived from a keyed hash, which are indistinguishable from real buckets, or state this residual under OQ-security-and-identity-15.

A default 24-hour maximum lifetime (target) that rejects longer `exp` will break imported deployments whose IdPs issue longer-lived service tokens. Say whether `ruralz bundle import` flags this, and state whether the maximum lifetime is measured as `exp` minus now or `exp` minus `iat`, and whether clock skew applies.

Go has no per-object memory accounting, so 'compiled engine memory ... reported per snapshot' needs a method. Say that `ruralz bundle validate` measures it in isolation, for example as the heap delta around a single-threaded compile, and that Nodes report an estimate. Also say what the 64 MiB ceiling (target) does to the 2 s compile budget (target) in System overview, which excludes cold Plugin compilation but not OPA or Cedar.
'no literal keys in `config`' is now phrased well. Link it explicitly to OQ-wasm-plugin-system-4 option (b), Node-resolved secret fields, so the two documents agree once that question closes.

blocking.section: Observability principles (aggregates and sharding) / Cardinality and overhead budgets (Overhead per signal)
blocking.issue: Still unresolved from the last round. The rule for which families shard still goes by label kind rather than by how many requests reach a label set. Gateway-scoped Policies reach every Route: the Configuration model worked example has five, `cors-default`, `jwt-default`, `ratelimit-global`, `headers-security` and `geo-block-default`. Every request on the Node therefore records into the same `ruralz_filter_duration_seconds{policy, phase}` label sets. In the SM-4 reference scenario, and on any Node dominated by one Route, every request also records into the same `ruralz_http_requests_total{route}` and `ruralz_http_request_duration_seconds{route}` label sets. Under the current rule these are 'other label sets' and get one unpadded atomic per value. At 32 P every core bounces the same bucket, `_count` and `_sum` cache lines. A cross-core line transfer costs about 100 ns (hypothesis), while the 2 µs budget for 40 operations leaves 50 ns per operation. The document also never says how a histogram `_sum` in seconds is added atomically. Go has no atomic float add, so a float64 sum needs a compare-and-swap retry loop, and that loop gets worse under contention. The contention the sharding was meant to remove therefore stays in the scenario where the Metrics row, SLO-GW-2 and SLO-GW-3 are measured.
blocking.evidence: Observability principles: "Only hot families shard: listener-scoped and enumeration-only families, at most 1,000 counter or gauge series and 64 histogram label sets (target), into S = min(`GOMAXPROCS` at start, 8) shards (target) padded to 64-byte cache lines." and "Other label sets use one unpadded atomic per value." Overhead per signal: "| Metrics | 2 µs or less (target) | 0 (target) | 24 MiB or less (target) |" and "15 metric operations in the SM-4 scenario and 40 for 10 Filters".
blocking.fix: Define hot by reach, not by label kind. Also shard the label sets of Gateway-scoped Policies, which are bounded by Gateway Policies × Phases, and the Route counter and histogram label sets of the first N admitted Routes (target). A simpler alternative is to shard every label set of the `fast` histogram families. Store histogram `_sum` as an integer count of nanoseconds or bytes, updated with `atomic.AddUint64`, and convert it at export. Add these shards to the metrics memory model, for example 2,000 Route histogram label sets × 192 bytes × 8 shards ≈ 3 MiB at S = 8 (hypothesis), then recompute the Metrics and All telemetry rows. Make the M1 contention benchmark run one hot Route with Gateway Policies at 32 P.

blocking.section: Metrics catalog (Gateway-added time)
blocking.issue: Still unresolved from the last round. The 32-interval cap cannot hold on ordinary traffic. Blocked body reads and client writes are excluded intervals, but copy work between them stays gateway-added. So in a pass-through copy, adjacent intervals never touch and never merge, and each chunk adds about two intervals. Any unary response of more than about 16 chunks (roughly 512 KiB at 32 KiB reads), and any trickling Upstream, goes over 32. Those requests are 'skipped and counted' and drop out of `ruralz_http_gateway_duration_seconds`. The SLIs of SLO-GW-2 and SLO-GW-3 then lean toward small bodies, and `interval_overflow` fills on normal traffic. Separately, parallel `aggregate` legs insert intervals from different goroutines into one pooled buffer, and the document does not say how that stays race-free without a lock on the request path.
blocking.evidence: Gateway-added time: "`ruralz_http_gateway_duration_seconds` is wall-clock time minus the union of excluded intervals: client reads and writes, upstream I/O, State Store round trips and declared remote calls (pack 8.7 rule 6)." and "Upstream I/O is time blocked on the Upstream (pooled-connection wait, dial, TLS, awaiting headers, blocked body reads and writes); Filters and copy work during a leg stay gateway-added. Intervals merge on insert, so parallel `aggregate` legs count once; a request keeps at most 32 (target) in a pooled buffer, beyond which it is skipped and counted."
blocking.fix: Replace the interval list with a constant-size accumulator. Keep a per-request excluded-depth counter and a timestamp. Each blocked section increments the depth on entry and decrements it on exit, and time is added to the excluded total only on the 0-to-1 and 1-to-0 transitions. That gives an exact union for sequential and parallel legs, uses per-request atomics and needs no cap. Then drop `ruralz_http_gateway_duration_skipped_total`, or keep it only for clock anomalies. If a list is kept, use it only for parallel composition and plain sums for sequential sections, because one goroutine's blocked sections never overlap.

blocking.section: Cardinality and overhead budgets (Overhead per signal, metrics memory model)
blocking.issue: Still unresolved from the last round. The metrics memory model budgets exactly one collection of live heap, but the budget is RSS and nothing bounds concurrent collections. By the document's own figures, the collection term (125,000 × 120 bytes ≈ 15 MB) is about two thirds of the 22.6 MiB. The OTLP periodic reader and every `/metrics` scraper each materialize one. An HA pair of Prometheus servers, the OTLP reader and an ad hoc curl can overlap, and each overlap adds about 15 MB, so memory grows with the number of scrapers. Also, 'Memory is RSS', but the arithmetic sums live bytes. With the default GOGC=100 and no GOMEMLIMIT, the heap target is about twice live heap, and collection output is short-lived garbage. About 23 MiB of live metrics state can therefore show as up to about 46 MiB of RSS. The 24 MiB Metrics row and the 40 MiB All telemetry row cannot be met as written.
blocking.evidence: Overhead per signal: "Memory is RSS above the 96 MiB idle budget (target) in [Tech stack and libraries](../engineering/01-tech-stack-and-libraries.md) (OQ-observability-17)." and "Metrics memory, checked by an M1 heap and contention benchmark at 4 P and 32 P, assumes 120 bytes per counter or gauge series and 300 per histogram label set, 64 × S and 192 × S more when sharded, and 120 per exported series in a collection (hypothesis). At the Node limit of 125,000 series, half histogram buckets, the unsharded part is about 22.6 MiB". Observability principles: "read by both exporters".
blocking.fix: Allow at most one collection in flight per process. Use single-flight so that concurrent scrapes share one encoded result, cached for up to 1 s (target), and have the OTLP reader either reuse that result or wait for it. A better option is to stream-encode `/metrics` straight from the aggregates into a bounded pooled buffer, so a collection costs a fixed buffer instead of 120 bytes per series. Then state the memory figures either as live heap times an explicit RSS factor, or under a documented GOMEMLIMIT or GOGC setting that the M1 benchmark uses. Recompute both rows and OQ-observability-17 to match.

blocking.section: Logging and access logs (Access logs) / Cardinality and overhead budgets (Overhead per signal)
blocking.issue: Still unresolved from the last round. The access-log queue memory budget contradicts the record size the document allows. 4 MiB for 8,192 records is 512 bytes per record, yet `host` and `path` alone may take 256 + 1,024 = 1,280 bytes. On top of that come a `User-Agent` with no stated length, names, IDs, the `failure_modes` list and the `ai` object. A burst of long-path requests fills the queue at about 1.5 KiB or more per record, 12 MiB or more in total. That is three times the row and pushes All telemetry past 40 MiB. If pooled records instead reference request strings rather than copying them, each queued record keeps its request's header block alive, up to the 256 KiB process ceiling in Data plane, which is far worse.
blocking.evidence: Access log fields: "| `method`, `host`, `path`, `truncated` | No query string; `host` and `path` cut at 256 and 1,024 bytes (target), flagged in `truncated` |" and "| `user_agent`, `tls_version` | Truncated `User-Agent`; TLS version |". Overhead per signal: "| Access log, logged request | 2 µs or less at p99, `when` included (target) | 8 or fewer (target) | 8,192-record queue, 4 MiB or less (target) |". Access logs: "The request goroutine evaluates `when` and fills a pooled record for a worker to encode; a full queue drops with a counter."
blocking.fix: Bound the queue by bytes as well as by records. Reserve each record's actual size from a 4 MiB (target) byte budget and drop with `reason="queue_full"` when the budget is exhausted. Records MUST copy truncated fields into their own pooled buffer and never reference request memory. Give `User-Agent` a length, for example 256 bytes (target), and cap `failure_modes` and the `ai` object. Alternatively, keep a record count only and set the memory row to 8,192 × the maximum record size.

blocking.section: Cardinality and overhead budgets (Cardinality budget)
blocking.issue: Still unresolved from the last round. Folding a retiring label set into `_overflow` together with its accumulated value creates increments that never happened. When the retiring ceiling is hit, a counter or histogram that has accumulated, say, 10 million requests or 5,000 5xx disappears, and `_overflow` jumps by that amount in one step. `rate()` and `increase()` over `_overflow`, and every `sum(rate(...))` panel over the family, then show a spike of events that never occurred in that window. SLO SLIs on per-resource families can fold this way. SLO-GW-4 reads `ruralz_plugin_call_overhead_seconds{policy, phase}`, and SLO-AI-1 sums over `provider` and `model`, so the spike feeds burn-rate rules and can page falsely. The claim that SLO SLIs never fold covers only listener and enumeration families, which is not true of these two.
blocking.evidence: Cardinality budget: "A Node-wide ceiling of 25,000 retiring series (target) caps a Node at 125,000 series: beyond it the oldest retiring sets fold into `_overflow`, values and late records included; per-Revision admission ignores retiring sets, so live folding stays identical on every Node." and "Listener and enumeration families, including SLO SLIs, are admitted first and never fold." SLO definitions: "| SLO-GW-4 | `ruralz_plugin_call_overhead_seconds` bucket `le=\"0.00005\"` / `_count` |" and "| SLO-AI-1 | 1 − M / (`ruralz_ai_settlements_total` + M) ... both summed over `provider` and `model` |".
blocking.fix: When a retiring set folds, end its series: stop exporting it and let OTLP and Prometheus staleness close it. Send only records that arrive after the fold to `_overflow`, and never carry accumulated values over. Apply the same rule when a Hot Reload moves a live label set past an admission limit. blocking.section: Control plane observability / Grafana dashboards and SLOs (Alert rules)
blocking.issue: Still unresolved from the last round. Page-severity rules built on `increase()` over rare-event counters miss the first event, and the document claims the opposite. A counter series first created at 1 has no earlier sample, so `increase()` returns 0 and the page never fires. Examples are the first failed Rollout since the leader started and the first `RZ-CFG-027` NACK. L counters restart on every failover as new series from a different replica (`service.instance.id` changes), so a failure shortly after a leader change is lost the same way. `RuralzRolloutFailed` (page), the NACK half of `RuralzTampering` (page) and `RuralzAIProviderCredential` all depend on events that are rare by nature. The document never says that alerted label sets exist at 0 before their first event.

Alert rules: "expr: max by (cluster) (increase(ruralz_control_rollouts_total{state=\"failed\"}[15m])) > 0" with "labels: {severity: page}", and "max by (cluster) (increase(ruralz_control_nacks_total{code=\"RZ-CFG-027\"}[1h])) > 0" with "labels: {severity: page}".
blocking.fix: Require every enumeration label set that an alert rule references to be created at 0 before the first event: at process start, and for L series when leadership is acquired. non_blocking.suggestion: Each of the two per-Node token buckets is one shared atomic. Under OQ-observability-4 option (a), a client that sets the sampled flag on every request makes every request run a compare-and-swap on the parent bucket's cache line, which adds new contention on the request path. Split each bucket across the S stripes at rate/S and burst/S (target), and consult it with the request's stripe, as the metric shards are.

'A lock-free per-connection random source' cannot be both lock-free and safe when up to 250 HTTP/2 streams of one connection generate IDs concurrently. Use the top-level `math/rand/v2` functions, which draw from the runtime's per-thread ChaCha8 source without locks, or give each stream its own source. State that the 1 µs, 2-allocation unsampled budget includes ID generation.

'offset by the stream ID when multiplexed': client-initiated HTTP/2 stream IDs are all odd, so (base + streamID) mod S with S = 4 or 8 reaches only half the stripes on each connection. That matters behind a load balancer or mesh sidecar that multiplexes over a few connections. Offset by streamID >> 1 instead.

The sharded set is capped at 64 histogram label sets, but the listener and enumeration histogram families already use about 28 plus 4 to 14 per listener (gateway duration, two body sizes, TLS handshake, session duration by protocol, State Store `op`, activation `stage` × `size_class`), so a few listeners exceed it. `ruralz_http_listener_requests_total` alone can reach 150 counter series per listener. blocking.section: Response caching (rule 3); Failure matrix (State Store out of memory)
blocking.issue: This is a regression from the new store byte-rate cap. The cap scales per Node with N_published, or is a flat 1 MiB/s with no count, so its Cell-wide bound is N_serving x per-Node cap. That bound exceeds the 30% `maxmemory` headroom in two ordinary cases the text does not cover. (1) A count lag above 15-fold: 2% x N_serving / N_published > 30%. (2) File mode, where N x 10 MiB per interval exceeds 30% of the shard whenever maxmemory < N x 33 MiB. The document nevertheless says the result is "inside the 30% headroom". Overshooting a `noeviction` shard makes limit scripts fail: Rate Limits fail open, and `ai.token-budget` returns 503 Cell-wide for up to 25 h. This is the failure the rule exists to prevent.
blocking.evidence: "Between reads, each Node caps store bytes per shard at 2% of `maxmemory` per 10 s divided by N_published, else 1 MiB per second (target). The Cell adds at most 2% × N_serving / N_published of `maxmemory` per interval: 20% under a 10-fold count lag, 6% of a 16 GiB shard from 100 file-mode Nodes (hypothesis), inside the 30% headroom." Scenario A: an autoscale from 2 to 40 Nodes (N_published rises at most 10% per minute) lets the Cell add 2% x 20 = 40% of maxmemory in one 10 s interval. That is above the headroom from a 69.9% sample. Scenario B: 100 file-mode Nodes on a 2 GiB shard add 1,000 MiB, about 49%, per interval. 1,000 file-mode Nodes on a 16 GiB shard add about 61%.
blocking.fix: Give the Cell bound in general form, N_serving x per-Node cap x poll interval, and make it hold. (a) Add an absolute per-Node ceiling beside the N_published share: min(2% of maxmemory / N_published per 10 s, X MiB/s) (target). (b) Shorten the `INFO memory` poll once a shard passes 50%, for example to 1 s (target), which costs N reads per second per shard. (c) Add a MUST: when N x per-Node cap x interval can exceed 30% of maxmemory, as in file mode above a stated Node count per GiB, the operator uses OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-11 option (a) or disables `cache`. Also emit a startup warning. Restate the worked figures and the "State Store out of memory" matrix row with these bounds, tagged (hypothesis).

blocking.section: Response caching (Layout, Invalidation); Failure matrix
blocking.issue: Generation keys `rz:rc:{<U>}:gen` have no TTL. Entries, fill leases, GCRA keys and quota counters each state an expiry; generation keys do not. Any non-error unsafe method on a `cache` Route creates or bumps one, even when nothing for that URI was ever stored. The State Store runs `noeviction`, so these keys grow without bound with the number of distinct URIs that are written. They also sit outside the rule 3 store-byte cap and outside rule 2's skip, since bumps take a reserved queue slice. This breaks the System overview's "Bounded everything" rule, and it ends in the out-of-memory row: limits fail open and `ai.token-budget` returns 503 Cell-wide.
blocking.evidence:
Layout: "a generation key `rz:rc:{}:gen`, and per partition a tag `{:

}` ..."; Invalidation: "A non-error response to an unsafe method on a `cache` Route bumps the URI's generation key after commit, in that Cell"; "Stores use the post-commit queue (pack 8.7), with TTL of freshness plus the larger stale window" (entries only); "The State Store holding limit keys MUST run `maxmemory-policy noeviction`". Scenario: `PUT /v1/orders/{id}` on a Route with a `cache` Policy, at 1,000 distinct ids per second, creates about 86 million generation keys per day, roughly 8 GB per day at about 90 bytes per key (hypothesis). No TTL, rule or purge removes them.
blocking.fix: Have every bump script also set `PEXPIRE` to the maximum entry lifetime plus margin, 25 h plus 1 h (target). This is safe because every variant tagged with an older generation has expired by then, so a missing key may read as generation 0. Optionally bump only for Routes whose Policy stored at least once, tracked per Node. State the key's lifetime in the Layout row, and count generation keys in the "State Store out of memory" row.

blocking.section: Load balancing
blocking.issue: The balancer budget is a regression from the L1-4 fix. It is applied per rebuild, first come first served, so its outcome depends on build order and does not match the document's worked example. At boot or after a Revision swap, the first rings built take full-size 1 MiB rings until the 256 MiB budget is spent. Every later rebuild finds no room even at 64 virtual nodes per Endpoint (64 KiB) and falls back to weighted `random`. Most ring-hash Upstreams in a large Bundle therefore lose affinity, while a few keep oversized rings. The document instead claims that all rings shrink uniformly to 256 virtual nodes per Endpoint.
blocking.evidence: "A Node's balancer structures share a 256 MiB budget, copy-on-write peaks included (target). A rebuild exceeding it halves the ring's virtual nodes per Endpoint, down to 64, then falls back to weighted `random` with degraded reason `balancer_budget` ... 1,000 rings of 64 Endpoints, 1 GiB, shrink to 256 virtual nodes per Endpoint (hypothesis)." Scenario: 1,000 ring-hash Upstreams with 64 Endpoints each, built 8 at a time. Roughly the first 250 reach 1 MiB, and the remaining about 750 fall to `random` with `balancer_budget`. Only a uniform plan gives the stated 256 virtual nodes each (256 KiB x 1,000, about 250 MiB).
blocking.fix: Plan sizes when the Revision is compiled, not per rebuild. Compute one virtual-node count per Endpoint for all rings: v = clamp(floor((budget - schedules - copy-on-write reserve) / (16 B x total ring Endpoints)), 64, 1,024) (target). Then rebuild every ring at v, and fall back to `random` only when even v = 64 does not fit, in a stated order such as largest ring first. On Endpoint-set changes, recompute v with hysteresis so that one discovery update does not reshape every ring. Keep the worked example consistent with the rule.

non_blocking.section: Rate limiting / Decision path; Failure matrix (Ruralz Control unreachable, or no Node count yet)
non_blocking.suggestion: Local-only entries now run at the Policy's per-Node ceiling. A Control-mode Node without a count has the full limit as its ceiling, so during warm-up its keys past the 200-per-second budget are admitted at the full limit for 10 s each, without GCRA, while the State Store is healthy. That is well above the min(`requests`, 10) fail-open clamp the same row gives. Either apply the clamp to local-only entries when no count exists, or state this bound in the row and in OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-19 and -20.

A `quota` key has no local pre-filter, so one Consumer at more than about 100,000 requests per second (hypothesis), with a high or no `ratelimit`, puts every request's script on one slot. That saturates the shard and opens its breaker on every Node, just like the "Hot constant key" row, which names only `ratelimit`. Add `quota` to that row, or add a row of its own, and point to OQ-system-overview-15 (leases) as the long-term fix.

The Tech stack Rate limiting row still says "`EVALSHA` with `NOSCRIPT` fallback", while this document applies `failureMode` on `NOSCRIPT` and reloads off the request path, which is correct under pack 8.7 rule 1. Note that Nodes must not use rueidis' Lua helper, which retries with `EVAL`. Ask the Tech stack owner to amend the row so the two documents agree.

A lookup needs the URI's `Vary` names from a per-Node bounded LRU, and "else the Node misses and learns the names". Long-tail URIs such as `/products/{id}`, with far more ids than the LRU holds, will then miss on most Nodes even when an entry exists, and each miss costs an origin fetch. State the default when names are unknown, for example assume no `Vary`, or the Route's last-seen names, and let the script check them. Give the expected hit-ratio effect (hypothesis).

The hot-entry bound is per entry: N reads per second, 10% of a 10 Gb/s shard link for 128 KiB at 1,000 Nodes. K hot entries of that size on one shard cost K x 10%. Give the per-shard bound, or scale the 1 s hot-entry lifetime with entry size. Also say how "read twice within 1 s" is detected with bounded memory, for example a doorkeeper Bloom filter.

"never a key with a GCRA answer" overstates the effect of segmenting. First-seen keys within budget, up to 500 per second per Node, still enter the main segment and can evict idle established keys under CLOCK. Reword to "never a recently used key". Also bound `config.limits[]` length, or give the per-entry layout, since 64 B per entry does not fit a digest plus several buckets.

blocking.section: Health checking and outlier detection; Circuit breakers; Failure matrix (Zone lost, black-holed: pooled HTTP/2 connections)
blocking.issue: Part of the earlier L4X-1 is still open. The 2 s detection comes from `HTTP2Config` pings, which only the `net/http` transport has. gRPC Upstreams use the grpc-go client (Tech stack row 'gRPC upstream client | grpc-go v1.84.x'). The document gives them only 'client keepalive' with no interval. grpc-go raises any client keepalive `Time` under 10 s to 10 s, and a default grpc-go server sends GOAWAY `too_many_pings` to clients that ping more often than every 5 minutes. A black-holed pooled gRPC connection therefore hangs until `perTryTimeout`, which is 7.5 s under the proposed defaults. `timeout` is not in the default `retryOn`, so those attempts end as 504 `RZ-UP-003`. Separately, the per-Endpoint cap only leaves slots free when the lost zone holds under half the Endpoints. Each Endpoint's cap is 2 x its share, so a zone with half the Endpoints can hold every slot. That is the common two-zone case: 2 Endpoints, or 3 per zone in 2 zones, where the caps sum to 1,024. Failure scenario: a two-zone gRPC unary Upstream loses one zone at 1,000 attempts per second per Node. With `round-robin`, 500 attempts per second each hold a slot for 7.5 s, so the lost Endpoints reach their 1,024 combined cap in about 2 s. From then on healthy-zone attempts wait in the 256 pending slots and get 503 `RZ-UP-006` on every Node, until ejection at about 7.5 s. Pure HTTP/2 hits the same exhaustion at about 1,500 attempts per second with `round-robin`, or about 3,000 with `least-request`, for the 2 s to 3 s before ejection. The row's claim that 'the per-Endpoint cap keeps a third free' holds only for three equal zones.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling)
blocking.issue: New regression from the revision. The throttle now has max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) hash slots, a success cache that hits do not extend, and a full cache flush on every snapshot swap and revocation advance. Together these put an unstated ceiling on legitimate `auth.basic` traffic and cause a 429 storm after every configuration change. An operator cannot tell from the document whether `auth.basic` fits their workload. On a 4-core Node there is 1 slot, which verifies 10 to 20 credentials per second (hypothesis). Every active client must be re-verified every 60 s, so the Node sustains only about 600 to 1,200 distinct active credentials, while the success cache is sized for 10,000. After each Hot Reload or Rollout, or after any revocation entry (for example a JWT `jti` logout unrelated to basic auth), every cached client misses at once. Only 1 slot plus 4 waiters are admitted within the 1 s deadline, so nearly all other legitimate callers get 429 RZ-AUTH-007. Neither the capacity bound nor the flush storm appears in the residuals or in OQ-security-and-identity-15.

blocking.fix: (1) State the capacity: "a Node sustains about slots x 10 to 20 x 60 distinct active `auth.basic` credentials (hypothesis); `auth.basic` suits low-cardinality clients, and high-cardinality callers SHOULD use API keys or JWT". (2) Stop flushing the whole cache. On a snapshot swap, keep entries whose Consumer credential digest is unchanged in the new snapshot, and on a revocation advance evict only entries for the revoked usernames or digests. Or spread re-verification over time and state the resulting 429 bound (target). (3) Size the success cache to the sustainable rate, or state why 10,000 is correct. (4) Add the capacity bound and the flush behavior to the T1 residuals and to OQ-security-and-identity-15.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling, 'Unknown usernames' and 'Username bucket' rows)
blocking.issue: The new unknown-username rule claims that "timing reveals nothing", but the design lets an attacker enumerate usernames through the throttle state. All unknown usernames share one bucket, while each known username gets its own bucket with a burst of 10. An attacker first empties the shared bucket with a few junk usernames, then probes a candidate. An unknown candidate is delayed up to 2 s or refused with 429 RZ-AUTH-007. A known candidate still has a full bucket, so it is hashed and gets a 401. The status and latency differ, so a security engineer relying on the stated property is misled. The document also leaves undefined what happens to a known-username attempt once bucket creation hits its limit of 100 per second per Node (target): whether it is refused, shares a bucket, or gets no bucket.
blocking.evidence: Line 403: "Unknown usernames | One shared bucket and a dummy hash through the same queue, so timing reveals nothing". Line 405: "Username bucket | Burst 10, refill 1 per second, 64-shard LRU of 100,000 (target); created only after the hash queue admits an attempt, at most 100 per second per Node (target)".
blocking.fix: Either give each unknown username its own bucket in the same LRU, created under the same admission rule and creation cap as known ones, so throttle behavior does not depend on whether the username exists. Or keep the shared bucket, delete "so timing reveals nothing", and list username enumeration through throttle state as a T1 residual in OQ-security-and-identity-15. In both cases, state the outcome for an attempt that exceeds the bucket-creation cap, for example "429 RZ-AUTH-007 unhashed, counted by cause", and apply it to known and unknown usernames alike.

blocking.section: Request hardening (Pre-authentication throttling); Threat model (T1)
blocking.issue: This regression comes from the fix for the earlier L4S-1. Every undeclared username now shares one bucket, and that makes the status code reveal which usernames exist. An attacker keeps the shared bucket empty by sending about 1 attempt per second with random bogus usernames. Each candidate username is then probed with one wrong password. An undeclared name waits on the empty shared bucket and gets 429 RZ-AUTH-007. A declared name draws from its own full bucket, is hashed, and gets 401 RZ-AUTH-002. So 401 versus 429 tells the attacker whether a username exists, and probing undeclared names costs them nothing. The document claims the opposite. It is also silent on what a new username receives once the 100-per-second bucket-creation limit is reached, which could be a second oracle.
blocking.evidence: Line 403: "| Unknown usernames | One shared bucket and a dummy hash through the same queue, so timing reveals nothing |". Line 405: "created only after the hash queue admits an attempt, at most 100 per second per Node (target)". Line 406: "An empty bucket holds at most 2 waiters, 1,024 per Node, for up to 2 s (target); others get RZ-AUTH-007 with `Retry-After` at once".
blocking.fix: Remove the shared bucket. Give every presented username, declared or not, its own bucket in the same 64-shard LRU, keyed by HMAC-SHA-256 of the username under the per-process key. The 100-per-second creation limit (target) and the hash queue already bound memory and CPU, so the shared bucket is no longer needed. At the creation limit, answer declared and undeclared names the same way (429 RZ-AUTH-007 before any hash). Replace "so timing reveals nothing" with "so neither timing nor status reveals whether a username exists". If the shared bucket stays, state the enumeration residual in T1 and OQ-security-and-identity-15 instead.

blocking.section: Revocation (Expiry); Authentication (JWT and OIDC); Threat model (T2)
blocking.issue: This regression comes from the fix for the earlier L4S-3. A (issuer, kid) revocation entry now expires after the maximum token lifetime, the same as `jti` entries and subject cut-offs. That expiry suits tokens, not keys. Whoever holds a leaked IdP signing key can sign new tokens at any time, each with a fresh `iat` and an `exp` inside the 24-hour bound. If the IdP still publishes that kid in its JWKS when the entry expires, or publishes it again (slow IdP rotation, a stale IdP replica, a restored IdP backup), Nodes accept the leaked key again with no alert. T2 says the leaked key is mitigated by `kid` revocation, but the fix lasts only 24 hours (target).
blocking.evidence: Line 426: "A `jti` entry MUST carry the token's `exp`, capped at the maximum lifetime, and expires then; cut-offs and `kid` entries expire after that lifetime". Line 417: "an IdP key by (issuer, `kid`), forcing a JWKS refetch". Line 91: "| T2 | JWT forgery, leaked IdP key | TB-1, TB-10 | [JWT and OIDC](#jwt-and-oidc); `kid` [revocation](#revocation) |".
blocking.fix: Keep a `kid` entry until an operator removes it. Collect it automatically only after the kid has been missing from every fetched JWKS of that issuer for at least the 6-hour key clamp plus the maximum token lifetime (target). While the entry exists and a JWKS still serves the kid, report a degraded state and emit `credential.revoked` on collection. Count `kid` entries against the 100,000 cap (target) separately so a cap overflow can never displace them. Mark the T2 mitigation as pending OQ-security-and-identity-4.

blocking.section: Control plane security (Admin ports); Threat model (T14)
blocking.issue: This regression comes from the fix for the earlier L4S-7, and it contradicts the foundation pack section 8.4 and System overview TB-9. The new text requires a token only for scraping from off loopback, so `/metrics` over loopback needs no credential. On Kubernetes every container in a Pod shares loopback. That includes the loopback `ollama` sidecar that Secrets rule 6 allowlists and any injected mesh or logging sidecar. A compromised sidecar can therefore read `/metrics` from 9901 and 9902 with no credential, which reveals Route, Upstream, Consumer and error-rate data. The text also does not say what `/metrics` does when no metrics token is configured.
blocking.evidence: Line 480: "Tokens are compared in constant time, only over TLS or loopback; without the operator token, `/tap`, `/config/dump` and `/debug/*` are off, and off-loopback scraping needs a token." Pack section 8.4, 9901 row: "Only `/healthz` and `/readyz` MAY be unauthenticated". System overview TB-9: "the rest MUST require a token or mTLS".
blocking.fix: State that `/metrics` needs the metrics token, the operator token or an admitted client certificate on every interface, loopback included. If no admin credential is configured, only `/healthz` and `/readyz` answer and every other path returns 401. Add sidecar access over shared loopback to T14. If unauthenticated loopback scraping is intended, record it as a proposed amendment to pack 8.4 and TB-9 in OQ-security-and-identity-7, with the residual stated.

non_blocking.suggestion: Scope the client certificates that the `RURALZ_ADMIN_TLS_DIR` CA admits. If they get operator scope, a stolen Prometheus mTLS scraper certificate reaches `/tap` and `/config/dump`, which is the same theft path the metrics token split closed (T14). Give certificates metrics-only scope unless they come from a separate operator CA or carry a marked SAN.

State the capacity for legitimate traffic. With max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) slots at 10 to 20 verifications per second each, a 16-core Node checks about 40 to 80 credentials per second (hypothesis). With a 60 s success-cache TTL, that serves roughly 2,400 to 4,800 distinct active basic credentials per Node (hypothesis). Flushing the whole cache on every revocation-sequence advance, including unrelated `jti` entries, makes every active basic client re-hash at once. Flush only entries whose username was revoked (store the username HMAC next to the entry). Consider reserving part of the slots for usernames with a recent success, so an anonymous spray cannot take every slot.

Rule 6 misses some cloud metadata addresses: 100.100.100.200 (Alibaba Cloud) and 192.0.0.192 (Oracle Cloud classic). Add them. Add the Kubernetes service-account token path (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount) to the rule 5 start-up refusal list, because it is the Vault credential under Kubernetes auth and the credential of the `kubernetes` provider.

A non-loopback State Store URL with credentials but no TLS sends the Redis AUTH secret in cleartext. Anyone on the path can then tamper with entries, which reopens T10 for GCRA and Quota state that the entry MAC does not cover. Refuse readiness in that case, or name it as its own degraded state with its own metric, and link it to OQ-security-and-identity-29.

State how the Node handles four JWT cases: a token without `kid`, where every key of the issuer is tried and counted against the refresh limit; a key's `alg` must match its `kty`, so RS256 and PS256 cannot be swapped on one RSA key; a JWKS key's `use` and `alg` members; and token-type confusion, where an ID token is presented where an access token is expected under a shared audience (`typ` check under OQ-security-and-identity-1).
Say what a new username receives when bucket creation reaches 100 per second per Node (target), and make that response the same for declared and undeclared names.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: The regional relay row is out of line with the finalize rules. Finalize waits only for replicas (voters and non-voters), and a read-only relay is neither. After finalize, the relay feed carries N-format entries: the version-advance entry, migrations, new record types, and a full resync, because every replica truncates its log (rule 3) and the relay's last index then comes before the retained log. A relay still at N-1, which the row calls in policy ('one older'), therefore meets a Control Store version above its binary's and halts under rule 4. Its Region's Nodes then serve detached, with no delivery, Enrollment or revocation, until the relay is upgraded.
blocking.evidence: Skew table: "| Regional Ruralz Control relay, Planned (M4) | The replicas' minor or one older; upgrades after the replicas, before its Nodes | Two minors older; newer than the replicas | Same halt rule; form: OQ-system-overview-16 |". Rule 3: "Once every replica reports N and a 24-hour soak (target) has passed, an operator finalizes". Rule 4: "A replica meeting a Control Store version above its binary's, or an unknown entry type, stops before serving". Control plane and GitOps, Relay feed: "It streams committed entries ... or sends full state when that index precedes the retained log".
blocking.fix: Make relays report their binary version on the relay feed and add them to rule 3: finalize requires every replica and every relay to report N. Change the row's in-policy cell to 'the replicas' minor, or one older only while the Control Store version is N-1', and its upgrade timing to 'after every replica reports N and before finalize'. Add that step to Figure 2 between g and h. Cite the read-only relay that Control plane and GitOps already decided, not only OQ-system-overview-16.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: Rollback after finalize gives no order for Nodes that have already moved to N, and the documented pieces conflict. Upgrade order moves Nodes to N only after finalize. Rule 5 then restores an N-1 Ruralz Control, which leaves those Nodes 'newer than the Control Store version', outside policy with nothing defined about what they get. Returning them to N-1 first can be blocked: once a post-finalize Revision uses an N-only field, the binary rollback limit refuses the handover and a restarted N-1 Node stays not ready. An operator who follows rule 5 after Node upgrades has no in-policy path.
blocking.evidence: Rule 5: "After it, rollback is `ruralz control restore` of the pre-upgrade backup into an empty N-1 deployment". Upgrade order: "After finalize, Nodes take a Zero-Downtime Upgrade ... from N-1 to N." Skew table: "| Ruralz Control and Ruralz Gateway Nodes | N-1; N once the Control Store version is N | N-2 or older; newer than the Control Store version |". Binary rollback limit: "Once a Revision uses a field above N-1's levels ... a handover to N-1 is refused."
blocking.fix: Add one ordered sentence to rule 5. While still on the N deployment, roll out to every Cluster a Revision without N-only fields and let it reach `complete`, so Last-Known-Good is promoted. Then return every Node to N-1 by handover. Only then restore. Add an exception to the skew table if the procedure instead tolerates N Nodes against a restored N-1 Ruralz Control for the duration of the restore, and name Zero-downtime upgrades and hot reload and High availability and disaster recovery as owners of the steps.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: Rule 2's 'one commit yields one digest' guarantee, and the Semantic versioning table, allow Revision-changing bug fixes that no schema level gates. A minor may ship a 'bug fix changing a Revision'. Rendering 'at N-1's schema levels and defaults' does not reproduce N-1 output when N's renderer or canonicalizer changed, so N and N-1 leaders still produce different digests for one commit mid-upgrade, and `ruralz bundle push` gets RZ-CFG-027 depending on which binary leads. The same table also conflicts with Versioned surfaces and the Configuration model, which allow golden-corpus exceptions only for deliberate default changes that ship as a new schema level. In `ruralz/v1beta1` and `ruralz/v1`, a digest-changing fix also breaks 'defaults never change'.
blocking.evidence: Semantic versioning: "| Bug fix changing a Revision (with a golden-corpus entry); new feature, ... | No | Yes | Yes |". Rule 2: "It also renders Revisions at N-1's schema levels and defaults, so a commit yields one digest, feasible because each default change is a new schema level". Versioned surfaces: "Every release reproduces the golden corpus byte for byte, except entries recording a deliberate default change". Configuration model, Canonical form and Revision: "every release MUST reproduce it byte for byte, except entries that record such a change. Changing the serialization requires a new format identifier."
blocking.fix: Require every change that alters a digest, whether a default change or a render or canonicalization fix, to ship as a new schema level in `ruralz/v1alpha1`. In `ruralz/v1beta1` and `ruralz/v1` it ships only behind a new opt-in field or a new format identifier. Rendering at a level then reproduces that level's output byte for byte. State that CI runs the golden corpus at every level still inside the skew window. Reword the Semantic versioning row to match, and widen the `ruralz bundle push` skew row from 'no `ruralz/v1alpha1` default changed' to 'no schema level added'.

blocking.section: Release artifacts
blocking.issue: Applying `ruralz-crds.yaml` before the chart on every upgrade is not feasible when a release adds a served CRD version. When `ruralz.io/v1beta1` first ships, planned for M3 with `ruralz/v1beta1`, the updated CRD lists it as served while every conversion webhook replica still runs N-1 and cannot convert to it. The API server then fails every request in that version and, if the storage version changes in the same release, every write. The failure lasts through the whole rolling Ruralz Control upgrade. If objects are stored in the new version and the operator then rolls back by restore to N-1 (rule 5), the N-1 webhook cannot read them.
blocking.evidence: Release artifacts: "| Helm chart | `oci://ghcr.io/ravindu-rev/charts/ruralz` at the product version; `ruralz-crds.yaml`, applied before the chart on every upgrade | Kubernetes | Planned (M2) |". Migration tooling: "CRDs serve every served version through Ruralz Control's conversion webhook, Planned (M2), so non-storage versions depend on its availability." Figure 2 has no CRD step.
blocking.fix: Apply a CRD manifest that adds a served version only once every Ruralz Control replica runs N (after node g in Figure 2). Make a version the storage version no earlier than the minor after it is first served, so rollback by restore never meets a stored version that N-1 cannot convert. Removals keep the existing rewrite-and-prune rule. Put this in the Helm chart and CRDs skew row, and hand the procedure to Zero-downtime upgrades and hot reload.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew
blocking.issue: The 'alternatively' switch for Quota and Token Budget counters still splits counters. Nodes learn the minimum Node version at different times: over the Control Stream, or not at all while detached (P9). One Node can switch at reset R1 while another learns only after R1 and switches at R2, so for the whole window between R1 and R2 the two write different keys. For monthly Quotas that is up to 2x for a month, not 'None'. For Token Budget it breaks the 'admits only when the remaining budget covers the full reservation' rule (P8, pack 8.9). This is what remains of L1-3.
blocking.evidence: "| Quota and Token Budget counters, alternatively | Once the minimum Node version is N, every Node switches at the next window reset | None (hypothesis) |". OQ-release-versioning-and-compatibility-9: "How do Nodes learn the Cluster's minimum Node version ... (a) A new Control Stream field, operator-set in file mode".
blocking.fix: Drop the alternative for Token Budget, which then uses only the shared-hash-tag path. For Quota, make the signal carry an absolute switch window, published at least one full window ahead, so every Node that has the signal switches at the same boundary. Replace 'None' with the residual bound: up to 2x for one window per Node that has not received the signal by then (hypothesis), owned by Scalability and distributed state.

blocking.section: Semantic versioning (One product version table)
blocking.issue: The change table lets any minor release ship a 'Bug fix changing a Revision (with a golden-corpus entry)'. The Configuration model, a foundation document, allows only one exception to byte-for-byte golden-corpus reproduction: a deliberate `ruralz/v1alpha1` default change shipped as a new schema level. Any other change to the serialization needs a new format identifier. This document's own Versioned surfaces row and rule 2 of Ruralz Control upgrades rely on that narrower rule. A digest-changing render or canonicalization fix gated by no schema level breaks 'render at N-1's schema levels and defaults, so a commit yields one digest'. It also breaks the `ruralz bundle push` skew row, and in `ruralz/v1beta1` and `ruralz/v1` it breaks 'defaults never change'. This is the same defect L1-12 raised, and it is still in the text. Here it is flagged as a contradiction with the Configuration model and ADR-0003.

blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew (skew table, regional relay row; Ruralz Control upgrades rules 3 and 4; Figure 2)
blocking.issue: The relay row puts a relay one minor behind the replicas inside policy after finalize. It also says relays upgrade 'after the replicas', which can fall after finalize, since Nodes upgrade only after finalize. But the relay is subject to the 'Same halt rule', and the relay feed streams committed entries on 8092. After finalize that includes the version-advance entry and N record types or migrations, which rule 3 applies only then. An N-1 relay that follows the in-policy path therefore meets a Control Store version above its binary's and stops (rule 4), or receives N encodings it is not required to decode. Every Node that dials that relay loses Rollouts until the relay is upgraded. The finalize gate and Figure 2 count only replicas, so nothing stops an operator from reaching this state.

Figure 2: "g{\"Every replica, voters and non-voters, reports N?\"}". Control plane and GitOps, Relay feed: "It streams committed entries filtered to the relay's Clusters: plan and assignment state with `storeEpoch` and `assignmentSeq`, signed promotions, revocations, anchor sets and `clusterNodeCount`."

Relabel Figure 2 node g to "Every replica, voters and non-voters, and every relay reports N?" and add a node before g: "Upgrade relays to N". blocking.section: Control plane and data plane version skew (Ruralz Control upgrades rules 3 and 4, Upgrade order, Figure 2 node p)
blocking.issue: The one-minor-at-a-time rule is enforced only from one side. Rule 4 halts a binary that is older than the Control Store version, but nothing halts a binary that is too new. Two cases are unprotected. The first is an operator skipping a minor, such as N+1 binaries on a Control Store at N-1, a common mistake with image tags. The second is starting N+1 before every replica has reported its post-finalize snapshot, which rule 3 forbids. In both, the new binary starts and decodes snapshots and log entries older than its N-1 decode guarantee. Rule 3 says the leader 'refuses the next upgrade', but it does not say how: upgrading is an operator replacing a binary, and no refusal path, error code or halt is defined. Figure 2 node p has no 'no' branch. An operator therefore cannot tell what happens, or what they will see, when the precondition is unmet.
blocking.evidence: Line 172: "Every replica then forces a snapshot past that index, truncates its log and reports to the leader, which refuses the next upgrade until all have." Line 173: "A replica meeting a Control Store version above its binary's, or an unknown entry type, stops before serving". Line 171: "N binaries MUST decode every N-1 entry, record and snapshot." Line 184: "Ruralz Control moves one minor at a time (rule 3)". Figure 2: "p -- \"yes\" --> a" (no 'no' edge).
blocking.fix: Extend rule 4: "A replica whose binary minor is more than one above the Control Store version, or whose local snapshot predates the last version-advance entry, stops before serving and exports a metric. The leader rejects status reports from a binary newer than the Control Store version until every replica has reported its post-finalize snapshot, using an `RZ-CP` code that Control plane and GitOps registers. That is how it refuses the next upgrade." In Upgrade order add: "Skipping a minor is refused: upgrade through each minor in turn." In Figure 2 add the edge p -- no --> a wait node: "Wait: an N+1 replica would be refused and stop".

blocking.section: Unit and property tests (Required properties, Token Budget row)
blocking.issue: New regression, introduced by applying my earlier non-blocking suggestion, which misread the AI/LLM gateway. The Token Budget property now charges all of R for each attempt that reports no usage. The binding rule is different: pack 8.9 and the AI/LLM gateway Settlement table charge all of R once per request, plus the usage other attempts reported. R per attempt without usage is only a proposal in OQ-ai-llm-gateway-15, and the gateway says 'none applies before it closes'. The property's overshoot bound also leaves out the gateway's '(attempts - 1) x R per concurrent request' term. When a request is charged R + u against a reservation of R, the budget overshoots by up to (attempts - 1) x R. A model-based property that generates Provider Fallback therefore fails a correct implementation, and the per-attempt wording pushes implementers toward the unaccepted OQ-15 proposal.
blocking.evidence: Required properties, line 95: "| Token Budget | R is reserved only if the remaining budget covers it; per attempt, settlement charges reported usage once (all of R if missing) and releases only R's unused part; overshoot stays within the sum of concurrent input-estimate errors (hypothesis; SM-10), plus hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama` (OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17) |". AI/LLM gateway, Settlement: "| Attempt reached the provider, no usage read | ... | All of R once per request, plus usage other attempts reported |" and "OQ-ai-llm-gateway-15 also proposes R per attempt lacking usage ... none applies before it closes." Overshoot bound: "... plus (attempts - 1) x R per concurrent request ([Model routing](#model-routing); hypothesis), plus, while OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17 is open, hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama`." Pack 8.9 Settlement: "When usage is missing ... charge all of R".
blocking.fix: Replace the Property cell with: 'R is reserved only if the remaining budget covers it; settlement charges each attempt's reported usage once, plus all of R once per request when any attempt that reached the provider reported no usage, and releases the rest of R; overshoot stays within the sum of concurrent input-estimate errors (hypothesis; SM-10), plus (attempts - 1) x R per concurrent request (hypothesis), plus hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama` (OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17). If OQ-ai-llm-gateway-15 closes, the property follows it.' The replacement is about 20 words longer, and there is room in the length band.

blocking.section: Integration tests
blocking.issue: The required NOSCRIPT scenario contradicts foundation pack section 8.7 rule 1 and principle P3. It requires a second blocking State Store round trip for one Policy on one request: EVALSHA, then EVAL again after NOSCRIPT. Traffic management and resilience, the owner of the GCRA call, rules this out explicitly. There, NOSCRIPT applies `failureMode` and schedules a reload. An integration test written from this line would fail a conforming implementation and accept one that breaks the pack.

The Node reloads the script off the request path, and the next request's `EVALSHA` succeeds ([Traffic management and resilience](../architecture/09-traffic-management-and-resilience.md))." blocking.section: Integration tests
blocking.issue: This contradiction was missed in earlier rounds and is still present (L2-4 reports it too). The required NOSCRIPT scenario makes a second blocking State Store round trip for one Policy on one request: `EVALSHA`, then `EVAL` again. Foundation pack 8.7 rule 1 forbids that. Contributors who build the integration test from this line would fail a conforming implementation, which applies `failureMode` and reloads the script off the request path. The test would also pass an implementation that breaks the pack.
blocking.evidence: Integration tests: "- `EVALSHA`, the cached form of pack section 8.8's single GCRA `EVAL`, meets `NOSCRIPT` after a script cache flush and resends `EVAL` within the same deadline." Foundation pack 8.7 rule 1: "Before the response is committed, each Policy makes at most one blocking State Store round trip per request." docs/architecture/09-traffic-management-and-resilience.md: "Nodes `SCRIPT LOAD` every script at connect, reconnect and failover; `NOSCRIPT` applies `failureMode` and schedules a reload, so no request makes a second round trip (pack 8.7 rule 1)."
blocking.fix: Replace the bullet with: "- After a script cache flush, `EVALSHA` (the cached form of pack section 8.8's single GCRA `EVAL`) meets `NOSCRIPT`: that request applies the Policy's `failureMode` without a second round trip (pack section 8.7 rule 1), the Node reloads the script off the request path, and the next request's `EVALSHA` succeeds." blocking.section: Consistency and accuracy bounds
blocking.issue: The fail-open bound for derived ceilings leaves out the per-Node floor of one token that the owning Traffic management document applies. As a result the stated number understates real admission whenever 2 x requests < N_published. The Control-mode case of a Node with no count (clamp max(1, requests / 100)) has no row at all. This document owns the pack 8.8 bound, so a wrong number here is a design defect.
blocking.evidence: Line 353: "| Rate Limit, fail-open | Derived ceiling, OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-16 option (b) | At most N_serving / N_published × 2 × `requests` per aligned window (target) |". The Traffic management failure matrix says: "Unfloored buckets admit N_serving / N_published × 2 × limit per aligned window, one token per Node at least" and "fail-open admits N_countless × the clamp ... 10 × limit (hypothesis)". Worked case: `requests: 10` per `1s` on 100 Nodes gives max(1, 0.2) = 1 token per Node, so 100 per second (10 × limit), not the 20 the row states.
blocking.fix: Restate the row as 'At most N_serving × max(1, 2 × `requests` / N_published) per aligned window (target)' and show the 10-per-second-on-100-Nodes example. Add a row 'Rate Limit, fail-open | Control-mode Node without a count | At most N_countless × max(1, `requests` / 100) per window, plus the counted Nodes' share (target)'. Point CE-4 and CE-9 pass criteria at the corrected formula.

blocking.section: Distributed state catalog
blocking.issue: The document claims per-request GCRA keeps the Cell limit exact while the State Store is healthy. In the same section it recommends option (a) of OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-20, under which first-seen keys past the budget are admitted from local-only entries without any GCRA call while the State Store is healthy. The bounds table has no row for that over-admission, so the recommended design contradicts the stated guarantee.
blocking.evidence: Line 287: "GCRA runs per admitted request from Planned (M1) through Planned (M3), as pack 8.8 fixes, keeping the Cell limit exact while the State Store is healthy." Line 291: "This document recommends option (b) of OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-16, option (a) of -20 and option (c) of -19". Line 350 (healthy row): "At most `requests` per `window` sustained, and 2 × `requests` in one window". Traffic management step 3: "past it ... a 10 s local-only entry (target) at the per-Node ceiling ... without GCRA".
blocking.fix: Qualify line 287: exact for keys with a GCRA answer, conditional on OQ-scalability-and-distributed-state-11. Add a bounds row 'Rate Limit | Healthy State Store, local-only key under OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-20 (a) | At most N_serving × ceiling per window for the 10 s entry lifetime (target)'. Add a chaos experiment for a key-rotation flood, for example 'CE-15: 100,000 new keys per second (target); per key at most N × ceiling per window; the GCRA segment is not evicted'.

blocking.section: Consistency and accuracy bounds
blocking.issue: The healthy Token Budget overshoot bound is narrower than the bound the owning AI/LLM gateway document states. It drops the per-attempt term and the hidden-reasoning term, which contradicts a depends_on document.
blocking.evidence: Line 359: "| Token Budget | Healthy, `closed` | Overshoot at most the sum of input-estimate errors, SM-10, owned by [AI/LLM gateway](06-ai-llm-gateway.md#settlement) (hypothesis) |". The AI/LLM gateway Settlement section says: "overshoots a budget by at most the sum of input-estimate errors across concurrent requests (hypothesis; SM-10 ...), plus (attempts - 1) x R per concurrent request ..., plus, while OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17 is open, hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama`."
blocking.fix: Quote the AI/LLM gateway bound in full: 'sum of input-estimate errors across concurrent requests, plus (attempts - 1) × R per concurrent request, plus hidden reasoning above C on `gemini` and `ollama` while OQ-ai-llm-gateway-17 is open (hypothesis)'. Change CE-13's pass criterion to match.

blocking.section: Distributed state catalog
blocking.issue: The post-commit queue drains its classes in strict table order, so cache invalidations sit behind cache stores. Under sustained store load the invalidation class, which is only 10% of the queue, fills up and drops. That defeats the reserved slice that Traffic management relies on, because an invalidation must not drop. Plugin writes can starve entirely.
blocking.evidence: Line 326: "Eight writers per Node drain the classes in table order, pipelining up to 64 writes per batch (target)." The table order (lines 321 to 324) is Quota refunds and Token Budget settlement, then Cache stores, then Cache invalidations, then Plugin writes. Traffic management says: "Generation bumps get a reserved 10% of that queue and one retry (target)" and "invalidations must not drop".
blocking.fix: Drain order: settlement first, then invalidations, then stores and Plugin writes. Use weighted round-robin between the last two, for example 4:1 (target), so no class waits longer than one batch interval. Add a bound: 'an invalidation waits at most one batch behind settlement (target)'. Add a CE-6 variant that saturates cache stores and asserts zero `cache_invalidate` drops.

blocking.section: Distributed state catalog
blocking.issue: Unbounded memory. The Plugin-writes class of the post-commit queue has only an item cap and no byte cap, and neither this document nor WASM plugin system caps value size (WASM caps keys at 256 bytes only). The claim that caches and the queue add at most 128 MiB per Node is therefore false.
blocking.evidence: Line 324: "| Plugin writes | 9,600 items (target) | Drop per Plugin Policy |". Line 559: "these limits add at most 64 MiB for keys, 256 MiB for balancers and 128 MiB for caches and the queue (target)". WASM plugin system: "Limits (target): 256-byte keys, `ttlMillis` 1 ms to 24 h, 10,000 keys per Policy per Node per minute, one `onLog` write per request". No value limit is given. For example, 9,600 queued 1 MiB values hold about 9.4 GiB.
blocking.fix: Add a byte cap to the Plugin-writes class, for example 16 MiB (target), and to the settlement class. Propose a per-value cap for `state.write`, for example 64 KiB (target), as an Open question owned by wasm-plugin-system or through OQ-wasm-plugin-system-19. Recompute line 559 from every class's byte cap.

blocking.section: High availability
blocking.issue: Two capacity targets contradict each other. Autoscaling lets steady-state CPU reach 60%, yet the availability rule requires survivors to stay under 80% CPU after the largest zone is lost. With two zones, 60% becomes about 120%. With three zones it becomes about 90%. Only four or more zones satisfy both.
blocking.evidence: Line 141: "| CPU | Container CPU utilization | 60% over 2 minutes (target) |". Line 169: "A Cluster SHOULD run at least three Nodes in at least two zones (target), sized so that losing the largest zone keeps survivors under 80% CPU (target)."
blocking.fix: Derive the CPU scale-out threshold from the zone count: threshold = 80% × (Z - 1) / Z, which gives 40% for two zones and about 53% for three (target). Alternatively, require at least three zones with a 50% threshold, and state the formula in both places.

blocking.section: High availability
blocking.issue: The required Raft HA state diagram models fencing staleness as an alternative to candidacy instead of a condition that runs alongside it. A voter in a minority partition goes Follower to Candidate and loops in Candidate, so on this diagram it never becomes Stale and never sends Reconnect (rebalance). Its Nodes stay pinned to an isolated replica, which contradicts Control plane and GitOps: 'A replica without word from a leader for one election timeout ... is stale ... After 30 s stale (target) it sends Reconnect'. Both transitions also fire on the same timeout with hashicorp/raft defaults (1000 ms), so the diagram does not say which one wins.
blocking.evidence: Line 189: "Follower --> Candidate: no leader heartbeat within HeartbeatTimeout". Line 191: "Candidate --> Candidate: split vote or no majority, new election after ElectionTimeout". Line 194: "Follower --> Stale: leader contact lost for one election timeout". No transition leaves Candidate toward Stale or Rebalancing.
blocking.fix: Model fencing as a concurrent region: a Raft region (Follower, Candidate, Leader) beside a fencing region (Fresh, Stale, Rebalancing) whose clock runs on 'no leader contact' whatever the Raft state. Or add 'Candidate --> Stale: no leader for one election timeout' and 'Stale --> Rebalancing: stale for 30 s' for candidates too. State what a Candidate serves to its Nodes: the Stale rule.

blocking.section: Stateless data plane
blocking.issue: The inventory claims to be complete, but it omits per-Node state that the dependency documents and this document create. Acceptance criterion 3 requires every in-memory per-Node state, each with its bound and why losing it is safe.
blocking.evidence: Line 50: "This table is the complete inventory of in-memory per-Node state; new per-Node state needs a row here before it ships." These are missing: State client breakers per shard, the connections and in-flight call counter (the 8,192 ceiling, defined at line 330 of this document); Response Cache miss coalescing ("up to 4,096 keys (target)") and the revalidation queue ("256-entry queue"); the per-URI `Vary`-name LRU; the per-shard `INFO memory` readings behind store skipping; the first-seen budget counters; Semantic Cache per-Node concurrency caps; Plugin per-Policy key-rate counters ("10,000 keys per Policy per Node per minute"); and `/tap` buffers (Data plane Bounded resources).
blocking.fix: Add one row for each missing item, each with a bound, what rebuilds it and why losing it is safe. For example: 'State client breakers and connections | 2 + 8 per shard, 8,192 calls | New dials; breakers start closed | First calls pay one deadline, then the breaker reopens'. Or drop the word 'complete' and point to Data plane Bounded resources for the others.

blocking.section: Chaos experiments
blocking.issue: Some scale figures carry no (target) or (hypothesis) tag, which breaks the style guide section 4 rule.
blocking.evidence: Line 589: "| CE-9 | Scale from 10 to 100 Nodes in 2 minutes | Over-admission within the derived-ceiling bound | Planned (M2) |". Line 586: "| CE-12 | Hot key at 10 times one shard's capacity | Calls for it at most N × ceiling per window | Planned (M1) |".
blocking.fix: Tag each figure on its line: 'Scale from 10 to 100 Nodes in 2 minutes (target)' and 'Hot key at 10 times one shard's capacity, about 1,000,000 calls per second (hypothesis)'.

non_blocking.suggestion: The reason given for 'two Nodes on one host are unsupported' does not hold: the file lock is per ${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}, so two Nodes with separate data directories could both bind. The real reason is that SO_REUSEPORT and CBPF steering assume one Node per network namespace. Write it as 'Not planned' with that reason, and avoid the word '(un)supported'.

'Supported topologies are OQ-scalability-and-distributed-state-2' uses 'Supported', which style guide section 4 reserves. Rephrase as 'The topologies the redis driver accepts are OQ-scalability-and-distributed-state-2'.

The divided-Quota YAML puts a Bundle `Consumer` in the same stream as control-plane-only `Environment` and `Cluster`, which a Bundle rejects with RZ-CFG-017. Split it into two fences labeled 'Bundle file' and 'control directory or --environments file'.

OQ-scalability-and-distributed-state-11 calls option (c) of OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-19 a pack 8.8 amendment. Option (c) persists the Node count under ${RURALZ_DATA_DIR}, so it amends pack 8.11. Name both sections.

'Tenants per Cell: At most 10% of tenants (target)' contradicts the single-Region topology of one Cell. Scope it to deployments with ten or more Cells. Also fix the arithmetic '1,000,000, 60% of 16 shards at about 100,000 each', which comes to 960,000.

'Connections per shard 10 × N_serving, 10,000 at 1,000 Nodes' equals the Redis and Valkey default maxclients at the Cell's Node ceiling. Make raising maxclients a MUST above about 900 Nodes. Also state which Cell ceiling binds first at realistic per-Node stateful request rates: at 5,000 State Store calls per second per Node (hypothesis), the 1,000,000-call ceiling binds at 200 Nodes.

Define the 8,192 in-flight State Store call ceiling as counting until reply or connection reset, not until the caller's timeout. rueidis cannot retract an auto-pipelined command already written, so abandoned calls still occupy ring slots during a CE-3 brownout. Also state how many half-open probe calls the breaker allows.

'Autoscaled Control-mode Clusters SHOULD declare per-Node ceilings' needs sizing guidance. A declared ceiling c fails open at N_serving × c, so c must be sized for the maximum autoscaled Node count (limit / N_max) to keep the bound at the limit.

The failover-lag row assumes the TAT rolls back. A key first written within the lag window is missing on the new primary and restarts GCRA with a full burst τ, which allows up to `requests` extra. Add that case. Also add the release document's case of a Node rolled back to N-1 after lazy migration, which admits up to 2x for one window.

hashicorp/raft randomizes the follower timeout between 1x and 2x HeartbeatTimeout, and election adds ElectionTimeout jitter, so 'about 1 to 2 s plus election round trips' is optimistic. Say 1 to 3 s plus round trips (hypothesis), or cite the research derivation.
The answer to OQ-wasm-plugin-system-19 covers only the queue half of option (a). Also answer the namespace half (Environment name as namespace).
The 'Quota denial cache' bound is a TTL (60 s per key), not a size. Give an entry bound, or state that it shares the 1,048,576-entry key table.
Order the rows by ID (CE-11 to CE-14 are interleaved) so milestone gating is easier to scan.
